topic: Writing the README for an open-source inference engine entering a market with entrenched competitors
notes: WebSearch was unavailable in this run; DuckDuckGo/Mojeek returned bot-challenges or 403. Discovery was done through API surfaces that are not blocked: the arXiv Atom API (search + id_list), the Hacker News Algolia API, and the GitHub contents API, plus direct fetches of known-authoritative URLs.

Every competitor README was fetched from raw.githubusercontent.com on 2026-08-17 and its structure recorded from the live file, not from memory. Two sources returned 403 (acm.org artifact badging, mojeek) and one returned a certificate error (catb.org); none is load-bearing for any claim in the guide.

Semantic Scholar API rate-limited (429) on both attempts; the Steinmacher newcomer-barrier line of work is therefore cited only through arXiv:2101.08903, and the guide does not claim a quantitative documentation-abandonment rate because none was verified.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages? (NN/g, summarizing Liu, White & Dumais, SIGIR '10)
keyInsights: 205,873 pages, each with >=10,000 visits, >2 billion dwell times; dwell time follows a Weibull distribution
'Users often leave Web pages in 10-20 seconds'; 'first 10 seconds of the page visit are critical'
Curve flattens only 'after people have stayed on a page for about 30 seconds'
'99% of web pages have a negative aging effect'
Prescription: 'communicate your value proposition within 10 seconds'
sources.usedFor: Part 1 - the actual size of the first-impression budget

sources.title: F-Shaped Pattern For Reading Web Content (NN/g, 232 users, replicated 2017)
keyInsights: 'The first two paragraphs must state the most important information'
'Start subheads, paragraphs, and bullet points with information-carrying words'
'They'll read the third word on a line much less often than the first two words'
sources.usedFor: Part 1 - front-loading; Part 7 sub-fold thesis anti-pattern

sources.title: Tuch et al., The role of visual complexity and prototypicality regarding first impression of websites (IJHCS 70(11), 2012)
keyInsights: Exposures tested: 50/500/1000 ms (study 1) and 17/33/50 ms (study 2), 119 real website screenshots
Both factors shape aesthetic ratings 'within the first 50 ms of exposure', detectable 'even within 17ms'
Low visual complexity + high prototypicality judged 'as highly appealing'
sources.usedFor: Part 1 - the first screen is judged before it is read; badge-count and density arguments

sources.title: Fan et al., What Makes a Popular Academic AI Repository? (EMSE 2020)
keyInsights: 1,149 academic AI repos; top 20% by stars vs bottom 70%, middle 10% as buffer; 21 features
Groups 'statistically significantly different in 11 of the studied features'
Strongest discriminators: number of links to other GitHub repositories in the README, number of images in the README, inclusion of a license
Highly cited papers more likely to have popular repos
sources.usedFor: Part 1.3 - the three measured discriminators; memra's missing figure (recommendation A4)

sources.title: Venigalla & Chimalakonda, Correlation between Readme Content and Project Popularity (2022)
keyInsights: 1,950 READMEs across ten programming languages
Popular projects' READMEs 'well organised using lists and images, and comprise links to external sources'
'contribution guidelines and references were observed to be associated with higher popularity'
sources.usedFor: Part 1.3

sources.title: Prana et al., Categorizing the Content of GitHub README Files (2018)
keyInsights: 4,226 hand-annotated sections from 393 randomly sampled repos; classifier F1 0.746 over 8 categories
'What' and 'How' content dominates; purpose and status information is frequently missing
sources.usedFor: Part 1.3 and Part 7.3 - status is the most commonly missing README category

sources.title: Borges & Valente, What's in a GitHub Star? (JSS 2018)
keyInsights: Survey of 791 developers plus the top-5,000 most-starred repos
'three out of four developers consider the number of stars before using or contributing to a GitHub project'
Explicitly warns about 'the risks faced when selecting projects by GitHub stars'
sources.usedFor: Part 1.3 - stars gate adoption but are a poor quality proxy

sources.title: Gao, Treude & Zahedi, Adapting Installation Instructions in Rapidly Evolving Software Ecosystems (2023/2025)
keyInsights: 1,163 README commits across 400 repos touching installation sections
Six change categories: pre-installation, installation, post-installation, help information updates, document presentation, external resource management
Template-augmented documents judged 'generally of better quality'
sources.usedFor: Part 5.4 - install sections drift most, and the drift is in prerequisites and verification

sources.title: Lipton & Steinhardt, Troubling Trends in Machine Learning Scholarship (ICML 2018)
keyInsights: 'failure to distinguish between explanation and speculation'
'failure to identify the sources of empirical gains' - e.g. crediting architecture changes for gains from hyper-parameter tuning
'mathiness: the use of mathematics that obfuscates or impresses rather than clarifies'
'misuse of language, e.g., by choosing terms of art with colloquial connotations'

sources.title: Dacrema, Cremonesi & Jannach, Are We Really Making Much Progress? (RecSys 2019)
keyInsights: Of 18 conference algorithms, 'Only 7 of them could be reproduced with reasonable effort'
6 of the 7 'can often be outperformed with comparably simple heuristic methods'

sources.title: Schaeffer, Kazdan & Denisov-Blanch, Min-p, Max Exaggeration (2025)

sources.title: arXiv cs.SE README corpus sweep (50 hits; 30 retrieved)
keyInsights: arXiv:1802.08391 - 43,900 npm packages: recurring themes are usage, install, license
arXiv:2502.18440 - minimal READMEs appear early; CONTRIBUTING only after contribution spikes
arXiv:2603.00331 (LintMe) and arXiv:2607.15780 (READU, 75% precision) - README defects are now machine-detectable, which is why a checkable checklist is the right artifact

sources.title: Gernot Heiser, Systems Benchmarking Crimes
keyInsights: 1.1 'Not evaluating potential performance degradation'; 1.2 'Benchmark sub-setting without strong justification'; 1.3 'Selective data set hiding deficiencies'
2.1 'Pretending micro-benchmarks represent overall performance'; 2.4 'No indication of significance of data'; 2.5 arithmetic mean for normalised scores
4.1 'No proper baseline'; 4.2 'Only evaluate against yourself'; 4.3 'Unfair benchmarking of competitors'; 4.4 'Inflating gains by not comparing against the state of the art'
5.1 'Missing specification of evaluation platform'; 5.2 'Missing sub-benchmark results'; 5.3 'Relative numbers only'
'Make your benchmarking rig part of your regression testing suite.'
sources.usedFor: Part 4.1 and Part 7.2 - the spine of the numbers discipline

sources.title: SIGPLAN Empirical Evaluation Checklist (Berger, Blackburn, Hauswirth, Hicks; ACM SIGPLAN EC, Oct 2018)
keyInsights: 7 categories, 22 items
Clearly Stated Claims: 'Claims not explicit', 'Claims not appropriately scoped', 'Fails to acknowledge limitations'
Suitable Comparison: 'Fails to compare against appropriate baseline', 'Comparison is unfair'
Adequate Data Analysis: 'Insufficient number of trials', 'Inappropriate summary statistics', 'No data distribution reported'
Appropriate Presentation of Results: 'Misleading summary of results', 'Inappropriately truncated axes', 'Ratios plotted incorrectly', 'Inappropriate level of precision'
sources.usedFor: Part 4.1, Part 7.2; the model for a category-based checklist

sources.title: MLPerf Inference Rules (MLCommons)
keyInsights: 'Results that cannot be replicated are not valid results.'
'The same system and framework must be used for a suite result or set of benchmark results reported in a single context.'
'SUT parameters and configuration must be uniquely and specifically named in the submission results.'
'Truncating output tokens to boost performance or meet accuracy is not permitted.'
Sorting samples beyond dataset boundaries and hard-coding query counts are disallowed
System diagram and software/hardware versions required 'sufficient for reproducibility'
sources.usedFor: Part 4.1 - reporting discipline; latency-bounded throughput as the serving metric

sources.title: Lee, Ten simple rules for documenting scientific software (PLoS Comput Biol 14(12), 2018)
keyInsights: Rule 3 'Include a quickstart guide' - without one, newcomers 'may abandon your tool'
Rule 4 'Include a README file with basic information' - treat it as the project homepage
Rule 9 'Write error messages that provide solutions or point to your documentation'

sources.title: GitHub Docs - About READMEs
keyInsights: 'A README is often the first item a visitor will see when visiting your repository.'
'any content beyond 500 KiB will be truncated' when rendered
Auto-generated table of contents via the 'Outline' menu icon
Relative links are rewritten branch-aware; 'we recommend using relative links to refer to other files within your repository'
Precedence: .github/, then root, then docs/
sources.usedFor: Part 1.2 mechanics

sources.title: Art of README (Kira)
keyInsights: 'The ideal README is as short as it can be without being any shorter.'
Cognitive funnelling: 'a funnel held upright, where the widest end contains the broadest more pertinent details'
Order sections by how fast they let someone 'short circuit' and bail
Badges are 'easy to abuse' and add visual noise
Inline anything essential, since the repo will outlive its host and external links
sources.usedFor: Part 7.1 badge racecar; Part 6.3 two-tier split

sources.title: standard-readme specification
keyInsights: 'Must not contain broken links.'
Short Description 'Must be less than 120 characters', must be on its own line, must not start with '> '
Table of Contents required unless the file is under 100 lines
Required order: Title, Short Description, ToC, Install, Usage, Contributing, License (License last)
sources.usedFor: Part 7.1 broken links; Part 9 item Z1

sources.title: Make a README
keyInsights: 'Use examples liberally, and show the expected output if you can.'
Description is 'a good place to list differentiating factors' versus alternatives
A stalled project should note status at the top so others may fork
sources.usedFor: Part 5.1 expected output; Part 7.3

sources.title: Open Source Guides - Starting an Open Source Project
keyInsights: The four questions: what does it do, why is it useful, how do I get started, where can I get help
READMEs 'explain why your project matters, and what your users can do with it'
'Goals can help you figure out what to work on, what to say no to'
sources.usedFor: Part 1.4 - and the argument that four questions are insufficient for an inference engine

sources.title: Changelog - Top ten reasons why I won't use your open source project
keyInsights: Reason 1: no README - and the elements it names: Description, Installation instructions, Where to get help, Contribution guidelines, Contributor list, Credits/Inspiration/Alternatives
Reason 7: unclear licensing - publishing publicly does not place code in the public domain
Reason 2: no tests/examples makes a project 'harder to trust'
sources.usedFor: Part 7 background. Dated (2011); seven of ten reasons are promotion advice, not README advice

sources.title: Lars Wirzenius - I'd like to review your README
keyInsights: 'A README is meant for someone who is first encountering the project', who should decide fast whether to dig deeper
Needs 'a very short, dense summary of the project aimed at someone who doesn't know anything about it yet'
'A README is not the manual, but it may have an example of how to typically use the software'
sources.usedFor: Part 6.3 two-tier split

sources.title: Papers with Code - ML Code Completeness Checklist (NeurIPS 2021 official guidelines)
keyInsights: Five items: dependencies, training code, evaluation code, pre-trained models, 'README file including table of results accompanied by precise commands to run/produce those results'
Analysis of >200 ML repos: repos checking more items 'tend to have a higher number of GitHub stars'
All five items: 'median of 196 and mean of 2,664 stars'
Users who cannot install dependencies 'are likely to give up on the rest of your code as well'
sources.usedFor: Part 1.3 - the only quantified link between reproducibility artifacts and adoption found in this run

sources.title: OpenSSF Scorecard - checks documentation
keyInsights: License check: file must exist, be top-level, and name an FSF/OSI license
Maintained: archived scores lowest; roughly weekly commits over 90 days scores highest; repos under 90 days not assessed
Separately scored: CI-Tests, Signed-Releases, Security-Policy, Packaging, Code-Review, Contributors
'a low score is therefore not a definitive indication that the project is at risk'
sources.usedFor: Part 1.3 - the machine-computed trust signals third parties publish about you

sources.title: NVIDIA - H100 + TensorRT-LLM inference performance (response to AMD MI300X claims)
keyInsights: 'The results shared did not use optimized software, and the H100, if benchmarked properly, is 2x faster.'
The delta was software config: vLLM v0.2.2.2 FP16 vs TensorRT-LLM v0.5.0/v0.6.1 with FP8 including FP8 KV cache; same workload (Llama 2 70B, 2048 in / 128 out, TP=8)
Both reproduction command lines published
'Industry-standard benchmarks like MLPerf also measure performance with this fixed response time metric.'
sources.usedFor: Part 4.5 - the canonical same-hardware-different-software 2x case; Part 4.6 competitor-column discipline

sources.title: Thinking Machines - Defeating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference
keyInsights: The cause is not atomics: 'in the typical forward pass of an LLM, there is usually not a single atomic add present'
'our forward pass lacks batch invariance' - output depends on the batch a request landed in
1000 temperature-0 completions produced 80 unique outputs, first diverging at token 103; batch-invariant kernels made all 1000 identical, at 26s -> 42s
Requirement: 'the reduction order for each element must be fixed regardless of the batch-size of the kernel'
sources.usedFor: Part 2.3 - why memra's byte-identical exactness gates are a differentiator a 2026 reader already understands without explanation

sources.title: vLLM - GPU installation documentation
keyInsights: Compiling kernels 'introduces binary incompatibility with other CUDA versions and PyTorch versions' - 'even for the same PyTorch version with different building configurations'
ROCm wheels are Python 3.12-only; otherwise the installer 'will silently fall back' and fails with 'libcudart.so: cannot open shared object file'
'Building from source requires GCC/G++ >= 11.3'; CUDA 13 images need 'an R580 or newer driver'
'vLLM does not support Windows natively.'
'NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs (B200, GB200) require a minimum of CUDA 12.8'
sources.usedFor: Part 5.3 - the catalogue of CUDA install hazard, and why memra's 'do not require nvcc' clause is worth more than a Docker image

sources.title: Martin Tournoij - Curl to shell isn't so bad

confidenceNotes: All 20 README structural descriptions come from live fetches on 2026-08-17 and are dated in the guide; they will drift and should be re-fetched before being quoted as precedent.

The 10-second / 30-second timing numbers are from web-page dwell-time research, not from a study of GitHub repository pages specifically. No study of repo-page dwell time was found. The guide states the transfer explicitly rather than implying repo-specific measurement.
The Papers-with-Code stars finding is correlational, not causal, and is described as such.

Four arXiv identifiers in the 2603-2607 range appeared in the live API feed but their dates were not independently verified; they are used only for corroborating patterns (README linting, maintenance signals, MemPalace critique), never as the sole support for a recommendation.
gaps: No study of dwell time or scan path on a GitHub repository page specifically - the strongest available evidence is web-page-general plus README-content-correlational.
ACM Artifact Review and Badging (403) and the Steinmacher newcomer-barrier line via Semantic Scholar (429) could not be fetched; the guide does not rely on either.

No documented, publicly litigated benchmark dispute between two open-source inference engines was found (the AMD/NVIDIA case is vendor-vs-vendor). The Anyscale/LLMPerf methodology dispute did not surface in the HN index.
No measured effect size for 'expected output shown in quick start' on conversion - the recommendation rests on precedent (candle, llm.c, tinygrad) plus PLOS Rule 3, not on an experiment.
No evidence found on whether a figure/plot in a systems README specifically improves conversion versus stars; Fan et al.'s image finding is on academic AI repos.
